publication.note: The publication lane compresses the same ten nodes and answers none of the dialogue questions.

questions.analogue: Where does the proof of part (a) use that H has finite index, and why is nothing else available: without it, need any positive exponent with g^n in H exist?
questions.merge_note: Two dialogue threads, one from each reader, ask the same thing: where the hypothesis lives (ask-1795502265-357, ask-1795502266-360). They are merged into one obligation; the zai thread also notes the printed statement hides the hypothesis entirely.

teaching.reason: A student should see that the whole finiteness of the problem sits in one step and that the statement is false without it.

expert-reference.reason: An algebraist sees at once that the positive exponent comes from finiteness of the coset set.

formal-audit.reason: The Lean hypothesis is the FiniteIndex instance on H, consumed by exists_pow_mem_of_index_ne_zero; the audit lane should name both.

questions.analogue: By what argument does a positive n with g^n in H exist: pigeonhole on the cosets H, gH, ..., g^nH, or a library lemma?
questions.merge_note: The Lean proof cites the library lemma and the informal solution proves the pigeonhole argument; the telling should give the mathematics, with the lemma named for the audit reader.

teaching.reason: The pigeonhole pairing of cosets is short and is the kind of argument a student must be able to reproduce.

expert-reference.reason: The expert accepts the library lemma or the one-line pigeonhole without display.

formal-audit.reason: The audit lane should show that the cited lemma exists_pow_mem_of_index_ne_zero proves exactly this, matching the informal pigeonhole.

questions.analogue: How exactly does normality of H make k divide the index: quotient group of order [G:H], Lagrange on the coset gH, then the membership criterion at m = [G:H]?
questions.merge_note: The print omitted the quotient-group and Lagrange steps entirely; the dialogue thread ask-1795502266-359 is the evidence.

teaching.reason: The hinge of the problem is that normality upgrades the coset set to a group; that deserves explicit words.

expert-reference.reason: For an expert part (b) is one line of quotient group and Lagrange, and saying so suffices.

formal-audit.reason: The Lean proof reaches it through pow_index_mem under the Normal instance; the audit lane should tie that lemma to the Lagrange route.

questions.analogue: Why package the exponents as the set T = {m : g^m in H} instead of arguing with a least positive k and the division algorithm directly?
questions.merge_note: Nobody asked this in the dialogue, but the proof needs it: T packages the least-k and division-algorithm steps into one subgroup statement and delivers all integers m, negative ones included, at once.

teaching.reason: The student's default is a minimal k plus division algorithm; seeing them as one subgroup of Z is the lesson.

expert-reference.reason: Unlike the a97A02 omissions, which were standard facts, this is the proof's single structural idea; a reference proof that hides it gives the reader nothing to retain.

formal-audit.reason: In Lean the packaging is literal: T is the comap of zpowersHom g, and the audit lane should show that comap.

questions.analogue: Why would a 3-cycle not serve as the counterexample in S_3?
questions.merge_note: For a 3-cycle g, the least positive exponent is 1 or 3, and both divide the index 3, so the conclusion of part (b) would hold and nothing would be refuted. The informal solution flags this trap in its difficulty discussion.

teaching.reason: The reflex first try is a 3-cycle; explaining why it fails teaches how to search for counterexamples.

expert-reference.reason: An expert sizing up S_3 rejects the 3-cycle instantly; the reference gives the working counterexample only.

formal-audit.reason: The audit lane should record that the chosen element has order 2 by orderOf_eq_prime and that the index is 3 by card_mul_index, so 2 does not divide 3.
